lessons.title: Power BI Fundamentals
lessons.description: The Power BI workflow: Get Data, Transform, Model, Visualise, Share.
lessons.theory_md:
## Power BI Fundamentals

### Why Power BI, when you already know SQL and Excel?
You already know how to query data (SQL) and calculate with it (Excel). Power BI's job is different: it turns that data into something a decision-maker can explore themselves, interactively, without ever writing a query — and it does this at a scale Excel starts to struggle with (millions of rows, live-connected to a database).

### The three tools that make up Power BI
- **Power BI Desktop** — where you build. Free, installed on your PC. Everything below happens here.
- **Power BI Service** — the browser-based home for publishing and sharing what you built.
- **Power BI Mobile** — a phone/tablet app for viewing published reports on the go.

You build in Desktop, publish to Service, view anywhere.

### The five-stage workflow — the shape of every project
1. **Get Data** — connect to Excel files, SQL databases, web APIs, folders of CSVs, and dozens of other sources.
2. **Power Query** — clean and reshape the raw data (covered in depth next lesson). This is the same *idea* as Excel's Power Query, and if you've cleaned data in pandas, the transforms will feel familiar too.
3. **Data Model** — define how your tables relate to each other (covered in "Data Modelling & Relationships"). This is conceptually identical to the JOIN logic you already know from SQL — you're just drawing it visually instead of writing `ON a.id = b.id`.
4. **Report View** — build the actual charts, tables, and interactive elements business users will click through.
5. **Publish** — push the finished report to Power BI Service so others can access it without needing Desktop installed.

### Your first look at the interface
When you open Power BI Desktop, three icons on the left sidebar matter most:
- **Report view** (the default) — your visual canvas, page by page.
- **Data view** — inspect the actual rows in each loaded table, like a read-only spreadsheet.
- **Model view** — see and edit the relationships between your tables.

### Why this workflow order matters
Doing these steps out of order is the single most common cause of a frustrating Power BI experience. Cleaning data in Power Query *before* modelling saves you from building relationships on messy columns. Building the model *before* the report saves you from re-doing visuals every time you fix a relationship. Follow the order above, in that order, every time.

**Business context:** A sales director who can't write SQL should still be able to open a Power BI report, click "North Region," and instantly see every chart update. That self-serve exploration — with zero risk of them ever seeing or breaking the underlying query — is the entire value proposition of this tool.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **SQL**: the Get Data -> Data Model -> Report workflow mirrors how you'd query (SELECT), then join (JOIN), then present results - same pipeline, visual instead of code.
- **Excel**: if you've used Power Query or PivotTables in Excel, the underlying engine here is genuinely the same one, just in a dedicated tool built for it.

exercises.prompt: List the five stages of the Power BI workflow in the correct order and briefly describe what happens at each stage.

quiz.question: What is the fundamental difference between a Power BI 'dataset' and a 'report'?
options: They are the same thing with two names
A dataset is the underlying data model; a report is the visual layer built on top of it
A report contains the raw data; a dataset contains only charts
Datasets are for Excel, reports are for Power BI
quiz.explanation: The dataset is your data model (tables, relationships, measures); the report is the visuals built to explore and present that model - one dataset can support many different reports.

quiz.question: Which Power BI tool would you use to clean and reshape messy data before it enters your model?
options: Power Query
DAX
Bookmarks
Row-Level Security
quiz.explanation: Power Query is where transformations happen - splitting columns, removing duplicates, fixing types - all before the data ever reaches your model.

quiz.question: What is DAX primarily used for in Power BI?
options: Formatting visuals with color
Writing calculations and measures against your data model
Connecting to a database
Publishing reports to the web
quiz.explanation: DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) is the formula language for building measures and calculated columns - it is to Power BI what formulas are to Excel.

lessons.title: Power Query in Power BI
lessons.description: Clean and shape data before it hits the model — the right place to fix messy data.
lessons.theory_md:
## Power Query in Power BI

### Same tool, same job as Excel — bigger stage
If you completed Excel's Power Query lesson, almost everything here will feel familiar — it's genuinely the same engine under the hood. The difference is scale: Power BI's Power Query routinely handles millions of rows pulled live from a database, not a few thousand rows in a workbook.

### Where cleaning belongs: before the model, not after
Transform data in Power Query (**Get Data → Transform Data**), never in DAX. This is a rule, not a preference: Power Query transformations run once, at refresh time. DAX measures recalculate on every single click a user makes in the report. Doing cleanup work in DAX means paying that computational cost over and over, forever — cleaning it once in Power Query is dramatically more efficient.

### Applied Steps — your undo-able recipe
Every transform you apply appears as a step in the **Applied Steps** panel on the right, in order. Click any earlier step to see exactly what the data looked like at that point — this makes Power Query far safer to experiment in than it looks; nothing is destructive until you click Close & Apply.

### The essential transforms
```
Remove Duplicates → ensures one row per key (e.g. one row per patient_id)
Replace Values    → fix typos: "Online " → "Online"
Split Column      → "John Smith" → "John" | "Smith"
Pivot / Unpivot   → reshape wide-format data to long, or long to wide
Merge Queries     → the visual equivalent of a SQL JOIN — combine two tables on a matching column
Append Queries    → the visual equivalent of a SQL UNION — stack two tables with the same columns
Group By          → aggregate rows, like SQL's GROUP BY
```
If you know SQL, every single one of these has a direct one-to-one equivalent you already understand — Power Query just does it with clicks instead of syntax.

### Writing your own transform: the M language
Power Query records every click as M code behind the scenes. You can also write custom columns directly:
```
= [Revenue] - [Cost]
= Date.Year([OrderDate])
= Text.Upper([ProductName])
```
This is the same logic as an Excel formula or a Python calculated column — same idea, different syntax.

### Incremental Refresh — for genuinely large tables
Once a table reaches millions of rows, reloading the *entire* table on every refresh becomes slow and wasteful. Incremental Refresh lets you set a date range parameter so Power BI only reloads new or changed rows going forward, not the whole history every time.

**Business context:** A finance team refreshing a 5-million-row transactions table every morning at 6am needs this to finish before the workday starts — incremental refresh is often the difference between a report that's ready on time and one that isn't.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **Excel**: this is the exact same Power Query engine as Excel's - everything transfers directly, just operating at a larger scale here.
- **SQL**: Merge Queries and Group By are Power Query's point-and-click equivalents of JOIN and GROUP BY.

lessons.title: DAX Basics
lessons.description: Calculated columns, measures and the most useful DAX functions.
lessons.theory_md:
## DAX Basics — Data Analysis Expressions

### The formula language of Power BI
DAX is to Power BI what formulas are to Excel — the language you use to calculate anything beyond what's already in your raw data. If you've written an Excel formula, DAX's syntax will feel familiar; if you've written a SQL aggregate function like `SUM()` or `AVG()`, the underlying concepts will feel very familiar too.

### Measures vs. Calculated Columns — the most important distinction to get right early
| | Measure | Calculated Column |
|---|---|---|
| Evaluated | At query/interaction time | Once, at data refresh |
| Responds to | Filter context (slicers, clicks) | Row context only |
| Storage | Not stored — calculated live | Stored in the model, taking up memory |

**Rule of thumb:** if the calculation should change as a user clicks a slicer (e.g. "Total Sales" that updates when they filter to North region), it's a measure. If it's a fixed value per row that doesn't depend on what's filtered (e.g. a "Full Name" column combining first + last name), it's a calculated column.

### Essential functions to know first
```dax
SUM(table[column])              -- total a column
AVERAGE(table[column])          -- same idea as SQL's AVG()
COUNTROWS(table)                -- row count, like SQL's COUNT(*)
CALCULATE(expression, filter)   -- re-evaluate an expression under a different filter — covered fully next lesson
DIVIDE(numerator, denominator, [alternate_result])  -- division that won't crash on divide-by-zero
RELATED(table[column])          -- pull a value across a relationship, like a JOIN would in SQL
```

### Your first real measure
```dax
Total Revenue = SUM(FactBilling[bill_amount])
Average Bill = AVERAGE(FactBilling[bill_amount])
Bill Count = COUNTROWS(FactBilling)
```
Create these by right-clicking a table → **New Measure**, then typing the formula. Once created, drag the measure onto any visual — it will automatically recalculate as the user filters the report.

### Why DIVIDE instead of the `/` operator
```dax
Margin % = DIVIDE([Profit], [Revenue])
```
If Revenue happens to be zero for some filter combination, `/` throws a visible error in your report. `DIVIDE` returns blank (or a value you specify) instead — always prefer it over a raw division symbol.

**Business context:** The exact same "average bill amount" you'd calculate with `AVG(bill_amount)` in SQL, or `AVERAGE()` in Excel, or `df['bill_amount'].mean()` in pandas — is `AVERAGE(FactBilling[bill_amount])` here. Four tools, one concept, four syntaxes. Once you notice this pattern, learning each new tool gets faster.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **SQL**: SUM(), AVERAGE(), COUNTROWS() are DAX's versions of SQL's SUM(), AVG(), COUNT() - same aggregation concepts, different syntax.
- **Excel**: DAX measures play the same role Excel formulas do - calculating something beyond what's in the raw data.

exercises.title: Write a DAX measure for Total Revenue
exercises.prompt: Write a DAX measure called 'Total Revenue' that sums the Revenue column from the Sales table.
exercises.hint_1: Measures are defined with: MeasureName = expression.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between a Measure and a Calculated Column?
options: They're identical in every way
A Measure is evaluated live based on filter context; a Calculated Column is computed once at refresh and stored in the model
Calculated Columns respond to slicers; Measures don't
Measures take up more memory than Calculated Columns
quiz.explanation: This is the single most important DAX distinction: Measures recalculate dynamically as a user filters/clicks, while Calculated Columns are fixed values computed once when data refreshes.

quiz.question: If you need a value that changes depending on which slicer the user clicks, should you use a Measure or a Calculated Column?
options: A Calculated Column, since it's stored and faster
A Measure, since it responds to filter context
Either works exactly the same
Neither — this requires Power Query
quiz.explanation: Only Measures respond to filter context (slicers, clicks, cross-filtering) — Calculated Columns are fixed once computed and won't react to user interaction.

quiz.question: DAX is described as being to Power BI what what is to Excel?
options: Charts
Formulas
PivotTables
Slicers
quiz.explanation: DAX is Power BI's formula language — the tool for calculating anything beyond what already exists in the raw imported data, just like Excel formulas.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Visual
lessons.description: Match the visual to the question — the difference between a chart that informs and one that confuses
lessons.theory_md:
## Choosing the Right Visual

Power BI has 30+ visual types. Most reports only need five or six, used well.

### The core set and when to use each
| Visual | Best for |
|---|---|
| Card | One headline KPI number |
| Line chart | Trend over time |
| Bar/Column chart | Comparing categories |
| Table/Matrix | Precise values the user needs to read exactly |
| Scatter chart | Relationship between two numeric measures |
| Map | Data with a real geographic dimension |

### Common mistakes to avoid
- **Pie charts with more than 4-5 slices** — humans can't compare angles accurately; use a sorted bar chart instead.
- **3D anything** — 3D distorts perceived size and adds zero information. Always use 2D.
- **Dual-axis line/bar combos** — easy to misread; only use when the two measures genuinely need different scales, and label axes clearly.
- **A gauge for something that isn't literally a target vs. actual** — gauges are consistently misread; a card with a comparison line is usually clearer.

### Formatting for clarity, not decoration
- Sort bar charts by value, not alphabetically — the eye reads rank order instantly.
- Use conditional formatting (data bars, color scales) in a Matrix instead of a separate chart, when the data is already tabular.
- One accent color for "the number that matters," neutral grey for everything else — don't rainbow every category.

### Tooltips and drillthrough
Right-click a visual → **Add Report Page Tooltip** lets you build a mini-report that appears on hover — useful for showing detail without cluttering the main page. **Drillthrough** lets a user right-click a data point and jump to a detail page filtered to exactly that context.

**Business context:** The wrong visual doesn't just look worse — it actively causes a stakeholder to draw the wrong conclusion. Chart choice is an accuracy decision, not just an aesthetic one.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **Excel**: the same chart-selection table (bar for compare, line for trend, scatter for relationship) applies identically — the tool changed, the visual grammar didn't.
- **Statistics**: a scatter chart here is the same statistical object as a scatter plot in the Correlation Analysis lesson — visually checking for a relationship before you ever compute Pearson's r.

exercises.title: Pick the right visual
exercises.prompt: You need to show monthly revenue for the last 24 months, and separately, the split of revenue across 8 product categories this quarter. Which visual would you use for each, and why?
exercises.hint_1: Think about what each visual is naturally good at reading.
exercises.hint_2: 24 months is a trend; 8 categories is more than a pie chart can handle cleanly.
exercises.hint_3: 24 months of revenue: a line chart, since it's a trend over time. 8 categories: a sorted bar chart, not a pie chart, since 8 slices is too many to compare by angle.
exercises.solution: Line chart for the 24-month trend (time series). Sorted bar chart for the 8 categories (too many for a readable pie chart; sorting by value makes ranking instantly clear).

exercises.title: Diagnose a bad chart
exercises.prompt: A colleague built a 3D pie chart with 12 slices to show market share by competitor. What's wrong with this choice, and what would you build instead?
exercises.hint_1: Consider both the chart type (pie) and the extra dimension (3D).
exercises.hint_2: 12 slices is far too many for a pie chart, and 3D distorts perceived size on top of that.
exercises.hint_3: Both 3D and too many slices make it unreadable. Replace with a sorted, 2D horizontal bar chart — easy to compare exact rank and size at a glance.
exercises.solution: Two problems stack: 3D distorts how large each slice looks, and 12 slices is far beyond what a pie chart can communicate clearly. A sorted 2D bar chart would let viewers compare competitors accurately at a glance.

quiz.question: Why does the lesson recommend against pie charts with more than 4-5 slices?
options: Power BI has a hard technical limit of 5 slices
Humans can't accurately compare angles beyond a small number of slices
Pie charts are always the wrong choice
It's a stylistic preference with no real basis
quiz.explanation: Comparing angles is a weak perceptual skill — beyond a handful of slices, a sorted bar chart communicates the same proportions far more accurately.

quiz.question: What should bar charts typically be sorted by?
options: Always alphabetically
By value, so rank order is instantly visible
Randomly, to avoid bias
By color
quiz.explanation: Sorting by value lets the eye read 'biggest to smallest' immediately — alphabetical order forces the viewer to hunt for the ranking manually.

quiz.question: What does Drillthrough allow a report user to do?
options: Change the underlying data source
Right-click a data point and jump to a detail page filtered to that specific context
Export the report to PDF
Automatically refresh the dataset
quiz.explanation: Drillthrough is an interaction pattern for going from summary to detail — the target page opens pre-filtered to whatever was clicked.

lessons.title: Data Modelling & Relationships
lessons.description: Build a star schema model that connects your tables correctly.
lessons.theory_md:
## Data Modelling & Relationships

### The model is the foundation — get this wrong and everything after is harder
The model determines what you're even able to calculate. A badly structured model makes every DAX formula a fight; a well-structured one makes most formulas almost write themselves. This is worth slowing down for.

### Star schema — the standard shape
- **Fact table** — the large table of transactions or events (e.g. every hospital bill, every sale). Has foreign keys pointing outward.
- **Dimension tables** — smaller lookup tables describing *who, what, where, when* (e.g. a table of patients, a table of dates, a table of products). Each has a primary key.

```
DimDate ──── FactSales ──── DimProduct
                │
            DimCustomer
```

If this looks familiar, it should — it's the exact same relational structure you already learned in SQL's JOIN lesson. A `FactSales` table full of foreign keys joining out to smaller dimension tables *is* what you were writing `INNER JOIN ... ON` statements against. Power BI just draws the relationship instead of you typing it every query.

### Creating a relationship
In **Model view**, drag a field from one table onto the matching field in another. Power BI detects the cardinality automatically in most cases:
- Primary key (unique values) → foreign key (repeating values) = **one-to-many** ✓ — this is the relationship type you want in almost every real model.
- Many-to-many relationships are usually a sign the model needs restructuring, not a feature to reach for casually.

### Cardinality reference
| Setting | When to use |
|---|---|
| One-to-many | The standard fact-to-dimension relationship |
| One-to-one | Splitting one logical table into two for readability |
| Many-to-many | Bridge tables, or "role-playing" dimensions used more than once |

### Cross-filter direction — the setting that causes the most confusion
- **Single** (the default, and almost always correct) — filters flow from the dimension table to the fact table. Click "North" on a region slicer, and every fact-table visual filters accordingly.
- **Both** — filters flow in both directions. This can produce results that look wrong (ambiguous filtering) if used without understanding exactly why. Reach for Single first; only switch to Both when you have a specific, well-understood reason to.

**Business context:** Exactly the same hospital patients/billing relationship you queried with `JOIN` in SQL — one patient, many bills — is the relationship you'd model here as one-to-many between DimPatients and FactBilling. The logic never changes across tools; only the syntax does.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **SQL**: a relationship here is exactly what a JOIN is in SQL - Power BI just draws the connection instead of writing ON a.id = b.id.
- **Excel**: this replaces the need for most VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP formulas once your model is built correctly.

exercises.hint_1: Think about what holds the measurable data.

quiz.question: In a star schema, what does the fact table contain?
options: Descriptive lookup data like customer names
The large table of transactions or events, with foreign keys pointing to dimension tables
Only date values
Nothing — it's just a placeholder
quiz.explanation: The fact table holds the measurable events (sales, bills, orders) — the 'what happened' — while dimension tables describe the who/what/where/when context around it.

quiz.question: What do dimension tables typically describe?
options: Only numeric totals
Who, what, where, when — descriptive context like customers, products, or dates
Nothing — they're optional and rarely used
The same data as the fact table, duplicated
quiz.explanation: Dimension tables are the smaller lookup tables (DimDate, DimProduct, DimCustomer) that give meaning and filtering context to the fact table's raw events.

quiz.question: Why does the lesson say to slow down and get the data model right first?
options: It has no real effect on later work
A badly structured model makes every DAX formula a fight; a well-structured one makes formulas nearly write themselves
Power BI requires a model before it will even open
Models can never be changed after import
quiz.explanation: The model determines what's calculable at all — poor relationships create incorrect or impossible calculations downstream, no matter how good the DAX is.

lessons.title: Report Design & UX
lessons.description: Build reports people actually use — layout, colour, and interaction patterns.
lessons.theory_md:
## Report Design & UX

### The 5-second rule
A business user should understand the main message of a report page within 5 seconds of looking at it — before reading a single label. If they can't, the page has too much competing for attention, or nothing is actually prioritized.

### Layout — the Z-pattern
Eyes naturally scan in a Z: top-left → top-right → bottom-left → bottom-right. Use this:
- **Top-left**: the single most important KPI card.
- **Top-right**: the primary trend chart (context for that KPI over time).
- **Bottom-left**: a breakdown (by region, by category — whatever explains *why*).
- **Bottom-right**: supporting detail.

Align every visual to a grid (**View → Snap to Grid**) — misaligned visuals are one of the fastest ways a report reads as unpolished, even when the data itself is solid.

### Colour — restraint is the skill
- Pick **one accent colour** for the metric that matters most on a page. Everything else should be a neutral grey.
- Colouring every visual a different colour looks decorative, not informative — it actively works against the 5-second rule.
- Reserve red/green specifically for conditional formatting (below/above target) — don't also use red/green decoratively elsewhere, or the meaning gets diluted.

### Slicers vs. Filters — a distinction worth getting right
- **Slicers** are visible on the canvas — the user sees and controls them directly. Use these for exploration you *want* the user doing themselves (e.g. "pick your region").
- **The Filters pane** applies a constraint invisibly — the user never sees or changes it. Use this for things you, the report builder, need fixed (e.g. "only show active accounts").

### Tooltips and Bookmarks — the two features that make a report feel "built," not just "assembled"
- A custom **tooltip page** (Page → Page type → Tooltip) shows rich detail on hover, without permanently cluttering the main canvas with every possible number.
- **Bookmarks** (View → Bookmarks) save a specific filter state, which you can then wire to a button — letting a user click "By Region" vs "By Product" and instantly reconfigure the whole page without touching a single slicer.

**Business context:** The same report, with good layout and restrained colour, gets used daily. The same data with a cluttered, rainbow-coloured, misaligned layout gets opened once and never again — design quality directly determines whether analytical work actually gets used.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **Excel**: the Dashboard Design lesson's layout and colour principles apply directly here, just in a more interactive canvas.
- **Business**: the Data Storytelling lesson's "lead with the insight" principle is what should drive every layout decision on this page.

lessons.title: Advanced DAX
lessons.description: CALCULATE, FILTER, time intelligence, and the measures that make Power BI powerful.
lessons.theory_md:
## Advanced DAX

### CALCULATE — the single most important function in DAX
`CALCULATE` re-evaluates an expression under a modified filter — it's the mechanism behind almost every non-trivial DAX measure you'll ever write.
```dax
Sales YTD = CALCULATE(
    SUM(FactSales[Revenue]),
    DATESYTD(DimDate[Date])
)

Sales North = CALCULATE(
    [Total Revenue],
    DimRegion[Region] = "North"
)
```
Read the second example as: *"Take the Total Revenue measure, but force the filter to only 'North', regardless of whatever the user has actually clicked."* This is how you build a fixed comparison point (e.g. "vs North") that sits alongside whatever the user is currently filtering to.

### Time Intelligence — comparing across time periods
This requires a proper Date table, explicitly marked as one (**Table tools → Mark as Date Table**) — Power BI's time functions depend on this to work correctly.
```dax
Revenue LY = CALCULATE([Total Revenue], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date]))
Revenue MoM % = DIVIDE([Total Revenue] - [Revenue LM], [Revenue LM])
```
`SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR` shifts the current filter back exactly one year — the same comparison a financial analyst does manually in Excel by referencing last year's column, just automatic and correct regardless of which period the user is currently viewing.

### Variables — making complex DAX readable
```dax
Revenue Growth =
VAR CurrentRev = [Total Revenue]
VAR LastYearRev = [Revenue LY]
RETURN DIVIDE(CurrentRev - LastYearRev, LastYearRev, 0)
```
Without variables, this same formula would need to repeat the `[Total Revenue]` and `[Revenue LY]` calculations inline, twice, making it both harder to read and slower to calculate (DAX would otherwise compute each measure reference separately). `VAR` computes each once, then reuses the result — always prefer this pattern once a formula has more than one moving part.

### A worked example, start to finish
Say you want "this month's revenue vs. the same month last year, as a percentage":
```dax
Revenue = SUM(FactBilling[bill_amount])

Revenue LY =
CALCULATE([Revenue], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date]))

Revenue YoY % =
VAR Current = [Revenue]
VAR Prior = [Revenue LY]
RETURN DIVIDE(Current - Prior, Prior, BLANK())
```
Each measure builds on the one before it — this layering (simple measure → time-shifted version → comparison) is the standard pattern for almost every real KPI you'll build.

**Business context:** "Are we up or down versus this time last year?" is one of the three most common questions any manager asks of any report. `CALCULATE` + `SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR` is how you answer it correctly, automatically, for every single filter combination a user might click into.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **Statistics**: the Time Series lesson's trend and moving-average concepts are exactly what CALCULATE + time intelligence functions implement here.
- **Business**: year-over-year comparisons built here are usually the exact KPI a stakeholder presentation leads with.

exercises.title: CALCULATE with filter
exercises.prompt: Write a DAX measure called 'Online Sales' that calculates SUM of FactSales[Revenue] filtered to where FactSales[Channel] equals 'Online'.

exercises.title: DIVIDE vs division
exercises.prompt: Why should you use DIVIDE([Profit],[Revenue],0) instead of [Profit]/[Revenue]?
exercises.hint_1: Think about what happens when Revenue is zero.
exercises.hint_2: Division by zero causes an error.
exercises.hint_3: DIVIDE handles divide-by-zero gracefully by returning the third argument (0) instead of an error.

quiz.question: What does the CALCULATE function fundamentally do?
options: Deletes rows from the model
Re-evaluates an expression under a modified filter context
Only formats numbers
Creates a new table
quiz.explanation: CALCULATE is the mechanism behind nearly every non-trivial DAX measure — it lets you override or add filters to change what an expression computes.

quiz.question: In `CALCULATE([Total Revenue], DimRegion[Region] = "North")`, what happens?
options: It sums revenue for every region combined
It forces the Total Revenue measure to always evaluate as if only 'North' were selected, regardless of the user's actual filter
It deletes all other regions from the model
It creates a calculated column
quiz.explanation: This is a fixed comparison point — useful for building 'vs North' style comparisons that stay constant no matter what the report user has clicked.

quiz.question: What's required for Time Intelligence functions like DATESYTD to work correctly?
options: Nothing special — they work on any column
A proper Date table, explicitly marked as a date table
A calculated column instead of a measure
Publishing the report first
quiz.explanation: Time intelligence functions depend on a contiguous, properly-marked Date table to correctly compute things like year-to-date or same-period-last-year.

lessons.title: Row-Level Security
lessons.description: Make sure each viewer of a shared report only sees the rows they're supposed to
lessons.theory_md:
## Row-Level Security (RLS)

One report, published once — but a regional manager should only see their region's data, not every region's. That's what Row-Level Security enforces.

### How RLS works
1. **Modeling → Manage Roles**, create a role (e.g. "Regional Manager").
2. Add a DAX filter expression on a table — this defines what rows that role can see:
```dax
[Region] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
```
Or, more commonly, a lookup against a mapping table:
```dax
[Region] IN VALUES(RegionAccess[Region])
```
3. Assign users (or groups) to the role in Power BI Service under the dataset's security settings.

### Static vs. dynamic RLS
- **Static RLS** — hardcode a fixed value per role (e.g. Role "North" → `[Region] = "North"`). Simple, but needs a new role for every region.
- **Dynamic RLS** — filter based on who's logged in (`USERPRINCIPALNAME()`), matched against a table mapping users to what they're allowed to see. One role, works for everyone — the standard approach for anything beyond a handful of fixed groups.

### RLS filters propagate through relationships
If RLS is applied to a dimension table (e.g. DimRegion), and that table has a relationship to the fact table, the filter automatically restricts the fact table too — you don't need to apply RLS separately to every table.

### Testing RLS before publishing
**Modeling → View As Roles** lets you preview the report exactly as a specific role would see it, without needing a second account. Always test this before publishing — an RLS mistake means either a security leak or a manager who mysteriously sees no data at all.

**Business context:** Any report shared across multiple departments, regions, or clients that shouldn't see each other's data needs RLS. Getting it wrong is a real business risk, not just a bug.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **SQL**: RLS is conceptually the same as adding `WHERE region = current_user_region` to every query automatically — Power BI just applies it for you at the model level instead of per-query.
- **Business**: this is a direct implementation of the stakeholder-awareness principle from Stakeholder Presentations — different audiences should see different levels of detail, and RLS enforces that at the data layer, not just the slide layer.

exercises.title: Write a dynamic RLS filter
exercises.prompt: You have a UserRegionMap table with columns Email and Region, linked to DimRegion. Write the DAX filter expression for a dynamic RLS role that restricts each user to only their assigned region(s).
exercises.hint_1: You need to match the logged-in user's email against the mapping table.
exercises.hint_2: USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns the current user's login; filter the mapping table by it, then check DimRegion is in that filtered result.

exercises.title: Static vs dynamic RLS decision
exercises.prompt: A company has 4 fixed sales regions that never change and about 15 regional managers total. Would you recommend static or dynamic RLS, and why?
exercises.hint_1: Consider how many roles you'd need to maintain under each approach, and how often the structure changes.
exercises.hint_2: With only 4 fixed regions, static RLS (4 roles) is simple to build and doesn't need a mapping table.
exercises.hint_3: Static RLS is reasonable here — only 4 roles to create and maintain, and the region structure is stable. Dynamic RLS becomes worth the extra setup once you have many users or the assignments change frequently.
exercises.solution: Static RLS is a reasonable choice here: only 4 fixed regions means just 4 roles to create, with no ongoing mapping table to maintain. Dynamic RLS earns its complexity when there are many users, frequent access changes, or dozens of possible values — none of which apply in this small, stable case.

quiz.question: What is the main difference between static and dynamic RLS?
options: They produce different security outcomes
Static hardcodes a fixed filter value per role; dynamic filters based on who's currently logged in via a mapping table
Dynamic RLS doesn't use DAX
Static RLS only works with numeric data
quiz.explanation: Static RLS needs one role per fixed group (simple, but doesn't scale); dynamic RLS uses the logged-in user's identity to look up their access, working for any number of users with one single role.

quiz.question: If RLS is applied to a dimension table connected to a fact table, what happens to the fact table?
options: Nothing — RLS must be applied separately to every table
The RLS filter automatically propagates through the relationship to restrict the fact table too
The fact table becomes completely inaccessible
The relationship breaks
quiz.explanation: Filters (including RLS filters) flow through model relationships — filtering the 'one' side of a relationship automatically filters the connected 'many' side too.

quiz.question: What does 'View As Roles' let you do before publishing?
options: Change who owns the report
Preview the report exactly as a specific role would see it, without needing a second account
Automatically fix any RLS mistakes
Export the report as a role-specific file
quiz.explanation: This is the essential pre-publish testing step — it lets you verify RLS is working correctly (not leaking data, and not hiding data that should be visible) before anyone else sees the report.

lessons.title: Performance Optimization
lessons.description: Keep large models fast — query folding, aggregations, and trimming model size
lessons.theory_md:
## Performance Optimization

A report that takes 15 seconds to respond to a click gets abandoned, regardless of how good the analysis underneath it is. Performance is a usability feature, not a nice-to-have.

### Query folding — push work back to the source
When Power Query transformations can be translated back into the source system's own query language (SQL, for a database source), the *source* does the filtering/aggregating instead of pulling everything into Power BI first. This is dramatically faster for large sources.
- Filtering, renaming, and basic type changes usually fold.
- Custom M functions, merges across different source types, and some text transformations often **break** folding.
- Check folding status: right-click a step → if "View Native Query" is available, that step is folding.

### Reduce model size
- **Remove unused columns** before loading — every column costs memory, whether or not any visual uses it.
- **Prefer Import mode aggregation tables** for huge fact tables — pre-summarize at a coarser grain (e.g. daily instead of transaction-level) for visuals that don't need row-level detail.
- **Disable auto date/time** (File → Options → Data Load) unless you need it — it silently creates a hidden date table per date column, which adds up fast on wide models.

### DAX performance
- Prefer `SUMX`/`CALCULATE` combinations that operate on fewer rows over iterating a huge unfiltered table.
- Avoid calculated columns where a measure would do — calculated columns are stored and recomputed on every refresh; measures compute on demand and never bloat the model.
- Variables (`VAR`) inside a measure prevent Power BI from recalculating the same sub-expression multiple times:
```dax
Margin % =
VAR Revenue = SUM(Sales[Revenue])
VAR Cost = SUM(Sales[Cost])
RETURN DIVIDE(Revenue - Cost, Revenue)
```

### Diagnose, don't guess
**Performance Analyzer** (View → Performance Analyzer → Start Recording → interact with the report) shows exactly how long each visual took and whether the time was spent in the DAX query or the visual rendering — fix what's actually slow, not what you assume is slow.

**Business context:** Large enterprise models with millions of rows and dozens of report pages live or die on performance discipline — this is precisely what separates an amateur build from a production-grade one.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **SQL**: query folding is the same instinct as filtering with WHERE before selecting — do the narrowing as early and as close to the source as possible.
- **Python**: avoiding calculated columns in favor of measures mirrors avoiding unnecessary intermediate DataFrame copies in pandas — compute only what you need, when you need it.

exercises.title: Diagnose a folding break
exercises.prompt: A Power Query step applies a custom M function to reformat a text column, and afterward, 'View Native Query' is no longer available on later steps. What likely happened, and why does it matter for performance?
exercises.hint_1: Think about what 'View Native Query' being unavailable indicates about where the work is happening.
exercises.hint_2: Custom M functions often can't be translated back into the source system's query language.
exercises.hint_3: The custom function broke query folding — from that step onward, Power BI has to pull the data locally and do the work itself instead of letting the source database do it, which is much slower on large sources.
exercises.solution: The custom M function broke query folding at that step. Once folding breaks, every subsequent step runs locally in Power BI instead of being pushed back to the source database — meaning all the rows get pulled across first, which is far slower for large source tables.

exercises.title: Measure vs calculated column
exercises.prompt: You need a 'Profit Margin %' value that should always reflect whatever filters/slicers the user has currently applied. Should this be a measure or a calculated column, and why?
exercises.hint_1: Consider which one responds to filter context and which one is fixed at refresh time.
exercises.hint_2: Only one of these two recalculates live as the user interacts with slicers.
exercises.hint_3: It should be a measure — measures recalculate live based on filter context (slicers, clicks), which is exactly what's needed here. A calculated column would be frozen at its refresh-time value and wouldn't respond to user interaction.
exercises.solution: This should be a measure. Measures recalculate dynamically based on whatever filter context the user has applied (slicers, cross-filtering), which is exactly the behavior needed. A calculated column is computed once at refresh and stored as a fixed value — it wouldn't update as the user interacts with the report.

quiz.question: What is query folding?
options: Collapsing visuals to save screen space
Power Query steps being translated back into the source system's own query language so the source does the work
A way to compress the .pbix file
A DAX function for combining tables
quiz.explanation: When folding works, filtering/aggregating happens at the source (e.g. the database) instead of after pulling all the raw data into Power BI — much faster for large sources.

quiz.question: Why does the lesson recommend measures over calculated columns where possible?
options: Calculated columns are deprecated
Calculated columns are stored and recomputed on every refresh, bloating the model; measures compute on demand without that cost
Measures are easier to write
There's no real performance difference
quiz.explanation: Calculated columns add permanent storage and refresh-time cost to the model; measures are computed only when needed, keeping the model leaner.

quiz.question: What does Performance Analyzer show you?
options: The list of all users who viewed the report
Exactly how long each visual took to render and where that time was spent
A history of past data refreshes
The DAX formulas used in each measure
quiz.explanation: Performance Analyzer gives real, measured timing per visual — the right tool for finding actual bottlenecks instead of guessing which visual is slow.

lessons.title: Publishing & Sharing
lessons.description: Publish to Power BI Service, manage workspaces, and set up scheduled refresh.
lessons.theory_md:
## Publishing & Sharing

### From Desktop to the world: Publish
**Home → Publish → select a workspace.** This uploads your report (and the dataset behind it) to Power BI Service, where others can access it through a browser — no Desktop installation required on their end.

### The vocabulary of Power BI Service
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Workspace | A shared folder/team space — where reports and datasets live together |
| Dataset | The data model — separate from any report built on top of it |
| Report | The visual layer — the pages and charts a viewer actually sees |
| Dashboard | A single page of pinned tiles pulled from one or more reports |
| App | A packaged, polished version of a workspace, published for end-users who should never see the underlying build |

One dataset can support several different reports — this is exactly why keeping the model (Lesson: Data Modelling) clean matters even after you've built your first report; you're not starting over for the next one.

### Scheduled Refresh — keeping published data current
Once published, the report is a snapshot until you configure refresh:
1. Dataset settings → **Data source credentials** → sign in so the Service can reach the original source.
2. **Scheduled refresh** → set a frequency (up to 48 times a day on Premium capacity, 8 times a day on Pro).

### Sharing options, and when to use each
- **Share a report** — grants access to specific named users or security groups. The default, safest choice for anything containing real business data.
- **Publish to web** — generates a public URL with no login required. ⚠️ Never use this for anything containing real customer, financial, or employee data — anyone with the link can view it, forever, with no audit trail.
- **Embed** — puts the report inside SharePoint, Teams, or a custom web application, respecting the same permissions as Power BI itself.
- **Power BI App** — the cleanest option for a polished, end-user-facing deployment; it hides the workspace's internal structure entirely.

### Row-Level Security (RLS) — one report, personalized per viewer
```dax
[Region] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
```
Set this in Desktop (**Modelling → Manage Roles**), test it locally with **View as Role**, then assign real users to that role once published in Service. The result: every regional manager opens the exact same report and dashboard, but each only ever sees their own region's data — one build, personalized automatically per viewer.

**Business context:** This is the payoff for everything in this module — a report built once, modelled correctly, refreshed automatically, and shared securely to exactly the right audience, each seeing only what they're supposed to. That's the difference between a one-off analysis and a real production reporting system.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **Business**: the Stakeholder Presentations lesson's delivery considerations (who sees what, how it's revisited later) are exactly what Sharing and Row-Level Security solve here technically.

exercises.title: Dataset vs Report
exercises.prompt: You update the underlying data in your SQL database. After refreshing the Power BI dataset, do you need to republish the report?
exercises.hint_1: The report is separate from the dataset.
exercises.hint_2: Refresh updates the dataset; the report reads from the dataset.
exercises.hint_3: No — refreshing the dataset updates the data. The report automatically reflects the new data without republishing.

exercises.title: Publish to web risk
exercises.prompt: A colleague asks you to use Publish to Web for a report containing employee salaries. Should you? Why?
exercises.hint_1: Think about who can access a public URL.
exercises.hint_2: Anyone with the URL can see the data.
exercises.hint_3: No — Publish to Web creates a public URL accessible to anyone, which is inappropriate for sensitive data like employee salaries. Use share or embed with authentication instead.

quiz.question: What does 'Publish' do in Power BI Desktop?
options: Deletes the local file
Uploads the report and its underlying dataset to Power BI Service so others can view it via browser
Only exports a PDF
Sends the file by email automatically
quiz.explanation: Publishing moves both the report (visual layer) and dataset (data model) to the cloud-based Power BI Service, where viewers don't need Desktop installed.

quiz.question: What's the difference between a Dataset and a Report in Power BI Service vocabulary?
options: They're the same thing with two names
A Dataset is the underlying data model; a Report is the visual pages/charts built on top of it
A Report contains the raw data; a Dataset contains only charts
Datasets are only used in Excel, not Power BI
quiz.explanation: This separation matters because one Dataset can support multiple different Reports built on top of it, reusing the same underlying model.

quiz.question: What is an 'App' in Power BI Service terms?
options: A mobile-only feature with no desktop equivalent
A packaged, polished version of a workspace published for end-users who shouldn't see the underlying build
Another name for a Dashboard
A type of DAX function
quiz.explanation: An App presents a clean, curated experience to consumers — hiding the workspace's in-progress reports, drafts, and build clutter that collaborators see.
